text: 8:05 a.m. Your request to buy a stapler has cleared nine departments out of twelve. The tenth, Procurement, sent it back: "Please specify color." Do you?
The department secretary says the director did sign your document, but in blue ink. The rules require black. The director is on leave until March. Now what?
right: Find whoever signs on his behalf

text: Your project's sign-off sheet has 34 approvals. Number 33 belongs to a department that was reportedly dissolved last year. The box is empty. What do you do?
Legal returns your contract with one edit: change "within five days" to "in a period not exceeding five days." That restarts the entire approval cycle. Argue?
right: Argue it means the same thing

text: A logistics colleague whispers: "If you drop your request into the Urgent folder before 2 p.m., they look at it the same day. Keep it quiet." Use the hack?
The deputy director will sign your memo if you co-sign his, about moving his vacation. His new dates overlap with yours. Do you sign?
7:40 p.m. Notification: "Your request has been approved." You have no idea which request. Number 4471-B. Open it, or pretend you have it all under control?
left: Open it and figure it out

text: In the evening you do the math: getting your vacation approved took longer than the vacation itself. File for the next one right now, in November?
The Policy Office has issued a policy on approving policies. It's 48 pages, and everyone must sign that they've read it by lunch. Do you read it?
The internal mail courier brings back your own memo from a month ago, marked: "Return to sender for approval by sender." Approve it with yourself?
left: Sign it and send it back

text: The Risk Office asks you to assess the risk that your project's approval will drag on. Honestly, it's 100%, because they're the ones dragging it. Say so?
Finance won't sign off a 3,400-ruble invoice: "Need three competing quotes." It was a cake for the team's birthday party. Go find two more bakeries?
The approval queue says you're number 212. Next to it is an Escalate button. Last week, everyone who escalated got moved to the back. Press it?
Your desk neighbor heads out: "If the approval system asks about me, say I'm on my way." He's not on his way. He's at yoga. Cover for him?
The project lead texts at 9:10 p.m.: "Finance wants the business case by morning or the budget expires." It's a fifteen-page document. Start now?
The archive needs the original 2009 order before your business trip can be approved. You started here last year. Where do you even look?
A new colleague asks how to get a mouse approved. The honest answer takes forty minutes and will break his faith in humanity. Tell him?
Security wants approval for your access to your own reports folder. Without access you can't write the report on why you don't have access. What do you file?
right: Ask a colleague to forward it

text: The Change Board meets once a month. Your change: one number in a template. Next meeting is in 27 days. Just change it quietly?
Evening ping: "Your document was rejected. Reason: reason not specified." Restart the approval tonight or in the morning?
At home, your partner asks how your day went. You start explaining Legal's sign-off on Finance's sign-off and watch their eyes glaze over. Keep going?
Your boss says in the morning: "Let it run without approval for now. We'll backdate the paperwork." Backdating is a firing offense here. Agree?
The VP's assistant books "a quick 5-minute approval sync." The invite has 22 people and a two-hour slot. Do you go?
An internal auditor notes that your project has 12 approvals and the rules require 13. Which one is missing? He doesn't know, "but one definitely is." Go find it?
right: Ask him to find it himself

text: Procurement offers fast-track approval for an "internal fee": three hours of your team's time on their project. Pay up?
A colleague staying late offers: "I'll sign off for my boss, I have his password." Convenient and completely forbidden. Your answer?
Reminder: tomorrow at 8:00 a.m., "Quarterly approval schedule approval." You're the organizer. There's no agenda. Write one now?
In the elevator you end up next to the department head whose sign-off you've been waiting on for three weeks. Forty seconds to the 34th floor. Remind him?
New rule: requests must use the format approved by a format request. Format requests can only be filed in the new format. What do you do?
right: File in the old one and pray

text: Accounting wants the memo redone because your signature doesn't fit the box. The box is 2 cm. Your signature is 4. Practice a smaller one?
right: Ask them to widen the box

text: In one week the intern mapped every approval route in the company onto a single A0 sheet. It's terrifyingly accurate. Hang it in the hallway?
left: Hang it up for all to see

text: At the coffee machine a Finance colleague says: "I've got your request, but I'm waiting on my own vacation approval first." Help her with hers?
You realize you've started writing "requesting approval" in texts to your mom. Time to change something?
The guard won't let you leave with your laptop: no approved equipment exit pass. It's your work laptop, issued yesterday. What now?
8:20 a.m. Fourteen "Approved" emails and one "Rejected," all on the same document. The rejection came last. Who wins?
left: Deal with the one who rejected

text: The development director asks you to be an "Approval Acceleration Ambassador." No bonus, plenty of work, but you get a nice badge. Take it?
The Templates team sent a new memo template. The "Issue" field fits 40 characters; the "Approvers" field fits 4,000. Use it?
A colleague with 25 years here offers to show you the "secret path" — whom to call to get anything signed in a day. In return, help her with a spreadsheet. Deal?
Evening call with a regional branch: they'll approve your document if you approve theirs. Theirs is 80 pages of pure policy-speak. Swap?
Your kid asks you to sign their school planner. You catch yourself thinking, "Where's the routing slip?" How do you react?
Quality asks how to improve the approval process. The survey is anonymous, but you log in with your corporate account. Be honest?
A courier brings a folder as thick as a brick and waits in the doorway. Sticky note: "Sign every page." There are 312 pages. Start?
In the canteen line, a Legal colleague admits they review your contracts first "because you always bring cookies." Keep up the tradition?
The unit head asks why the project is stuck. You show the 12-step approval chart. He sighs: "I'm presenting on Monday." What do you offer?
right: Suggest he report it as is

text: HR asks you to sign your consent to the processing of your consent. One page, three copies. Sign?
8:15 p.m. The turnstile won't let you out: "Time on site exceeded. Overtime approval required." Everyone who could approve it has gone home. Now what?
A friend invites you to a 9 p.m. movie. Your document is queued for a director who only signs after 8 p.m. Wait for the signature?
Late in the evening the project chat argues whose sign-off goes first, Legal's or Finance's. The thread is 200 messages long. Step in?
The evening cleaner asks if she can toss the stack of papers on your desk. It's drafts from twelve approval rounds, with the signed originals somewhere inside. Toss it?
Morning email from the department director: "Why am I learning about this project from a sign-off sheet?" You sent him the deck three times. Remind him?
To get a pen from the supply room you need Form KD-17. The supply room is out of KD-17 blanks, which are issued only via Form KD-18. What do you fill in?
Morning bulletin: "From Monday all documents must use 12.5-point font." Your 200-page report is set in 12. Reformat it?
right: Submit as is, with a note

text: At 8:40 a teammate asks you to submit her timesheet: "I'm stuck in traffic and it closes at nine." Timesheets must be filed in person. Help her?
The methodology lead sends a "brief guide" to filling in trip reports. The guide is longer than your entire trip report. Study it?
left: Study it and redo the report

text: The annual employee survey asks: "Describe your role in one word from the approved list." Your word isn't on the list. What do you pick?
A Finance colleague sends a 47-tab spreadsheet: "Just tick the boxes, five minutes tops." Five minutes for her, maybe. Take it on?
HR wants you to re-sign your employment contract because your title has a hyphen in it, while the org chart uses a space. Sign?
A senior specialist from the Policy Office can't keep track of his own rules and calls you to check clause 4.7.2. You don't remember it either. Your answer?
The floor's scanner saves files in a format no company software can open. The report is due in an hour. What do you do?
Policy says you can leave at 6:00, but everyone stays till 8. You've finished everything by 5:55. Be the first to stand up?
right: Sit around till seven for show

text: In the evening you discover the leave form now demands "a handover plan agreed with your stand-in." You don't have a stand-in. What now?
A new evacuation plan arrives: the exit route goes through a meeting room that got blocked with filing cabinets last week. Report it?
right: Joke about it in team chat

text: You can't unsubscribe from "Policy Updates" because unsubscribing counts as a policy change. Thirty emails a day. Set up a filter?
The timesheet wants your day split into 15-minute slots. At 6 p.m. you realize half your day went into filling in the timesheet. How do you log that?
The team lead hands out the new weekly report form: "Done," "Not done," and "Why what's done isn't done." Fill it in seriously?
A new hire shows up with a stack of papers: "They said I can't get to my desk without the floor lead's sign-off." There is no floor lead. Is it you?
Health & Safety asks you to sign the log confirming you were briefed on stapler safety. There was no briefing. Sign anyway?
Records is renumbering every document from "2024-001" to "001-2024." All 600 references in your reports will break. What do you do?
The expense form wants the "purpose of spend." You bought water for meeting guests. Options: "hospitality," "facilities," "other." Which?
A pedantic colleague spots a typo in your email and cc's four managers. The typo was in the word "policy." Reply all?
The quarterly supplies order closes today. You must forecast how many paper clips you'll need until March. What do you write?
Certification wants you to confirm your desk meets the standard. The standard describes a desk that doesn't exist in the building. Your reply?
left: Send a photo of your desk

text: The intern stays until nine retyping a report to the new standard. He doesn't know the standard was scrapped at lunch. Tell him?
left: Tell him and send him home
right: Let him finish, it'll be useful

text: At home you're filling in a school form for your kid and instinctively look for the "Manager approval" box. Your partner laughs. Take offense?
10 p.m. email: "URGENT! Form F-12 is obsolete, use F-12/1." You submitted six F-12s today. Redo them?
The HR portal wants a new profile photo by end of day: "White background, no smiling." Everyone loves your smiling photo. Change it?
In the morning you find a cabinet labeled "Policies 2003–2011." The key is hanging right there. Inside could be the answer to your problem — or moths. Open it?
In the elevator, someone from Analytics offers: "Want a script that fills in your timesheet for you? Just don't tell anyone." Accept?
Ethics asks whether you're breaking policy by accepting candy from colleagues. Yesterday you got two toffees. Declare them?
right: Say you ate them on the spot

text: At the forms harmonization meeting, people debate whether the date goes top right or bottom left. It's been two hours. Speak up?
The division head bounces your report because of the "Signature" box. You signed, but you were also supposed to write the word "signature" next to it. Fix it?
Your digital signature has expired. Renewing it requires an application signed with a digital signature. How do you get out of this?
right: Ask your manager to sign it

text: Your desk neighbor keeps every company form in one tabbed folder. She'll share it if you cover for her at the stand-up. Deal?
left: Take the folder, cover for her

text: Standards review sends back your deck: the arrow on slide 7 isn't by the book, it's "freestyle." The client has already seen it. Fix it?
At 8:30 p.m. the night watchman sees you scanning documents and offers help: "My scanner at home is better." The documents are confidential. Your answer?
right: Thank him and chat a bit

text: Your sister calls in the evening for help with her tax return. You're so sick of forms that the word "field" makes your eye twitch. Help?
Before leaving you set an auto-reply. Policy requires your stand-in's name, phone, office and "a brief summary of their competencies." Comply?
left: Fill it in by the book

text: The company-paid evening course "Filling in Forms Properly" is mandatory. Tonight's topic: "The Notes Field: Friend or Foe?" Go?
right: Log in and do other stuff

text: Internal Comms wants an article titled "How I Learned to Love Policies" for the company magazine. Payment: a T-shirt. Write it?
The front desk won't accept your document because the paper clip is on the left. Policy says right. It's urgent. Move it?
In the job catalog your position is "Lead Specialist for Specialists." Nobody knows what it means, including you. Ask HR?
The company printer stamps "DRAFT" on every page, even final versions. The VP is waiting for the final. What do you do?
left: Roam the floors for a printer

text: You're invited to a working group on reducing the number of forms. Meetings: four hours every week. Join?
At 8:15 you're asked to sign the visitor log. You've worked here six years, but your badge won't beep. The guard won't budge. What now?
Planning sends the "Annual plan" form, due by 10 a.m. It's 9:20 and already November. How do you tackle it?
In the mornings the elevator to your floor only takes badges with Level B access. Yours is Level C. Walk up to the 27th?
right: Wait for a Level B rider

text: A colleague going on leave hands you a 90-page handover file with a quiz at the end. The quiz is mandatory. Take it tonight?
right: Take it when you need it

text: Mom calls in the evening: "You sound so tired. More reports?" Tell her you spent three hours choosing the "Other" field?
New rule: meeting rooms must be left "in their original state, per the photo." In the evening you're arranging chairs to match the picture. One is missing. Search?
left: Hunt the floor for the chair

text: In the evening you notice you know every form number by heart but can't remember your last aimless walk. What do you do?
8:00 a.m. The KPI dashboard is red: your "Index Engagement Index" is down 3%. Nobody knows how it's calculated. Dig in?
The KPI analyst asks everyone to log "three key results of the week." Your key result: survived Monday. Write it?
The boss announces a new goal: "Cut meetings by 20%." To that end, he's scheduling a series of meetings. The first starts in ten minutes. Go?
The mandatory training platform reminds you: 14 courses due this quarter, you've done 2. "Anti-Corruption" takes three hours. Start this morning?
Compliance quiz question: "A colleague offers you coffee. What do you do?" Every option is a trap; the right one is "report it to Ethics." Your pick?
A colleague admits she breezes through compliance courses with her eyes shut, clicking Next. She has more certificates than you. Try her method?
The Efficiency team sets your KPI: "Number of tasks closed." You could split one big task into forty tiny ones. Do it?
right: Keep it as one honest task

text: The team dashboard is up on the big screen. Your bar is the shortest because you spent the week helping other departments. People are glancing your way. Explain?
On a floor walk the VP points at your screen: "Why is your chart going down?" Because it's a cost-reduction chart. Explain?
An outside coach runs a session on "KPIs as a Lifestyle" and asks everyone to name a KPI for their downtime. All eyes on you. Answer?
Last evening of the quarter. You're one contract short of your KPI. The client will sign for a discount you're not allowed to give without approval. Do it?
9 p.m. notification: "Your Information Security course expires in three hours. Non-completion will be reported to your manager." The course takes 2.5 hours. Start?
Your neighbor at the country house says his job has no KPIs at all. For the first time this year you hear the word "relaxed." Ask about openings?
Before bed you open the dashboard "just to check." Forty minutes later you're still comparing shades of red. Close it?
Someone from another department texts at night: "Can you mark in the system that we did the training together? My KPI's on fire." You did it separately. Do you?
The VP's assistant announces: "Everyone must set their KPI as their desktop wallpaper." Yours is 47% complete. Do it?
left: Put it up, let them see
right: Set a kitten and forget it

text: At an in-person training, the compliance trainer acts out "the chocolate bribe" and casts you as the briber. Everyone's filming. Play along?
In the morning you receive a certificate for a course you never started. Clearly a system glitch. Report it?
You must fill in a KPI report on your KPI reporting. The KPI office measures how promptly KPI reports are submitted. You're a day late. Your excuse?
The project manager asks you to "tweak" the dashboard numbers before the chairman's review. Just a little. Twelve percent. Do you?
At an inclusion workshop the facilitator asks you to pair with someone you don't know. Forty thousand employees, and you land next to your boss. What do you do?
Employee survey: "How satisfied are you with the number of surveys?" It's the third survey this week. Your score?
Your desk neighbors race to finish the "Personal Data Protection" course first. The prize: the last slice of pie. Join in?
The Motivation team launches "KPI Star of the Month," with a photo by the elevators. You're second. First is your best work friend. Push to overtake him?
In the evening you watch the mandatory ethics video. The presenter talks about values so movingly that you start feeling guilty about that pen you took from a meeting room. Return it?
At dinner a friend asks how your work is measured. You start explaining the KPI system and lose yourself a minute in. Keep going?
8:30 p.m. email from Analytics: "There was an error in the KPI formula; all quarterly bonuses will be recalculated." Yours goes down. Write back now?
Your kid shows you a drawing titled "My parent at work." It's a person staring at a red chart and crying. What do you say?
left: Hug them and promise to ease up

text: The learning coordinator calls: "You finished a 90-minute mandatory course in 4 minutes. The system suspects cheating." How do you explain?
A new company metric tracks how much you type per minute in work chat. You're in the bottom 10%. Start typing more?
The office overachiever finishes every mandatory course on day one and emails everyone his certificates. Today's: "Modesty in the Workplace." Reply?
The Rollout team asks you to pilot the new OKR system. Three extra hours a week, but you'll be the first to watch it break. Agree?
The report generator errors out on every fifth KPI. You can recheck 300 rows by hand or add an asterisk: "data under review." Which?
Your direct report begs you not to fail him on the security course: "I'm just bad at tests, but I do the work." You know he's right. Your call?
left: Pass him on your own authority

text: The canteen trays now have QR codes for a five-minute "Healthy Eating" course. While you watch it, your soup is going cold. Finish the course?
Evening payslip: your bonus is exactly half what you expected. Reason: the "Course attendance" KPI. You were on sick leave. Appeal?
The team lead texts at 10 p.m.: "The committee reviews dashboards tomorrow. Ours dropped. Find a way to spin it as growth." Do you?
In the morning you realize you're measuring your sleep as "percentage of plan achieved." Today: 62%. What do you do with that?
left: Leave early and catch up on sleep

text: Your department came last in mandatory course completion. The boss asks you to personally call every straggler. There are 38. Start dialing?
9 a.m. pulse survey: "Rate your mood with an emoji." Five options, all smiling, just with varying enthusiasm. Which do you pick?
right: The biggest grin, to be left alone

text: In the morning the manager asks everyone to invent an extra "stretch" KPI. You stare at the empty line. What do you write?
The annual fire safety course at 8:30: find the extinguisher on your floor and photograph it. No one has ever seen it. Search?
A financial analyst wants your "five-year KPI forecast" this morning. You don't know what's happening next week. What do you send?
Learning & Development hands out badge pins for completed courses. You have one. Your neighbor has twenty and jingles when he walks. Catch up?
At the entrance, security checks whether you've done the access-control course. If not, your badge is suspended. You can take it on your phone at the turnstile. Do it?
Your partner proposes a phone-free evening. Twenty minutes in, your phone buzzes: "KPI updated." Look?
The team chat is buzzing tonight: the dashboard counts lunch and bathroom trips as idle time. Someone suggests a group complaint. Sign it?
At the gym your fitness tracker says "Daily goal 120% done." It's your only green KPI all week. Stay for another round?
Evening email: a guide on "How to Set KPIs That Can't Be Missed." It's by the very person who set your impossible ones. Read it?
Your neighbor says he took a time management course and now gets everything done. He offers you the link. It's 40 hours long. Sign up?
You open the portal to find a new org chart. Your department now reports to itself, two levels up. Your name appears in two boxes. Whom do you contact?
8:30 a.m. Meet the new boss. Third one this year. He asks each person for five minutes on "yourself, your tasks and your pain." What do you share?
The "Reorganization" email arrived at 7:58 a.m. and consists of one sentence: "Details to follow." The team chat is already panicking. Calm them down?
After the reorg your department moves from floor 12 to floor 31. Boxes must be packed by lunch. Your desk is a four-year archaeological dig. How do you pack?
right: Sweep it all into one box

text: Your former boss, moved to another department, writes: "Take my two best people, or they'll be cut." Take them?
right: Say no, you have no headcount

text: By the water cooler: in the new structure your team merges with the one you've been fighting over meeting rooms for three years. Prepare?
An outside consultant gives you an hour to describe "what value your department creates." Its survival depends on the answer. What do you write?
left: An hour of detail and numbers

text: One of your people asks point-blank: "Am I being cut?" You don't know, but you suspect there's already a list. What do you say?
You've been renamed from "Team Lead" to "Stream Leader." Same duties, same pay, but you must order new business cards at your own expense. Do it?
right: Cross out the old title by hand

text: A briefing explains the matrix structure: now you have two bosses, functional and project. They've already given you opposite tasks for today. Whose do you do?
After the merger, at the joint meeting, half the people sit by one wall and half by the other. Someone has to make the first move. You?
The Transformation Director wants one slide on how your work changes after the reorg. You don't know. Neither does he. What do you draw?
A colleague you've had lunch with for ten years is being laid off. Packing his box, he asks if you'll write him a reference. Right now?
right: Promise to do it this weekend

text: The updated org chart lands in the evening — version three today. You're back in your old department, but without a desk. Call someone?
A friend at another company sends you an opening: "We had a reorg in 2015, quiet ever since." Sounds like a fairy tale. Apply?
right: Save it for a rainy day

text: 9 p.m. in team chat: "Guys, I think they're moving us all to Novosibirsk." Source: a dream. Your reply?
Late at night your manager sends you a list of employees and asks you to "prioritize who stays." Due by morning. What do you do?
right: Ask to meet and discuss criteria

text: Your desk neighbor stays late and admits the reorg scares him more than the dentist. Stay and listen?
In the evening you catch yourself sketching your own org chart on a napkin, where you report only to yourself. Hang it at home?
Evening live stream on "the new operating model." The CEO shows 64 boxes and says, "It's simple." Ask a question in chat?
An HR officer brings a contract amendment first thing: "Change of organizational unit." Must be signed by ten. Read the fine print?
The office manager announces: after the reorg, floor 31 has fewer seats than people. "Flexible seating" — first come, first served. Show up at 7?
The new project office wants all your processes mapped in a notation nobody here knows. Training starts in a month. The deadline is next week. Now what?
Your two new bosses both summon you to 2 p.m. meetings in different buildings. Both say: "This is the priority." Where do you go?
left: Dial into one, attend the other

text: Three people from a restructured department join your team. They bring rituals: standing stand-ups and a team anthem. Your folks prefer sitting. What do you do?
right: Let each group do its thing

text: After the reorg your budget is "temporarily frozen pending structural clarification." A client order is burning. Borrow from the next team's budget?
left: Work it out with the neighbors
right: Tell the client there's a pause

text: Change Management asks you to be a "change agent," gathering colleagues' moods weekly. Colleagues think these agents are spies. Accept?
After the move, a cabinet with no owner sits in the corner. Inside: forty unopened mugs with the logo of the previous reorg. Hand them out?
The new department head wants each of your people's "strengths and weaknesses" by tonight. How do you write it?
The intern asks: "So who's my manager now?" You open the org chart together, and you both get lost. Your answer?
In the evening your daughter asks why your company keeps moving boxes around. You try to explain and realize you have no idea. Your answer?
right: Sit down and study the strategy

text: A recruiter friend calls: "Heard you're reorganizing. Want me to find you something without matrices?" Agree to an interview?
Former teammates from a dissolved department invite you to a "farewell to the department" dinner. Early start tomorrow. Go?
HR sends a "post-reorg survey" at 8:40 p.m. Last question: "Are you happy with your new role?" Nobody has told you your new role. Answer?
In the morning your office door has a new sign naming a department you've never heard of. Your key still works. Go in?
left: Go in and work as usual

text: At the morning meeting the team asks what happens to their bonuses after the reorg. You don't have an answer, but you can't stay silent. What do you say?
left: Promise to find out by Friday

text: The person who held your new role left a note: "Don't touch the third folder." The third folder is right in front of you. Open it?
At 8:10 a colleague in the parking lot asks, "Have you seen who's above us now?" You haven't. He doesn't say, just sighs. Pry it out of him?
You're invited to join a "self-managing pilot team": no bosses, but twice as many meetings. Join?
After the reorg your badge opens your new department's doors but not the restroom on your floor. An access request takes five business days. What do you do?
In the morning, your old team invites you to "their" breakfast in the canteen, though you're formally in another department now. Your new team is eating too. Join whom?
Overnight the intranet rewired every link to the new structure. Your bookmarks lead nowhere, including the report due at 10 a.m. Where do you look?
At the new department's morning meet-and-greet, everyone shares "a fun fact about yourself." Your only fact: you've survived four reorgs. Share it?
The new director's assistant wants "everything you need from the director, in one list, by 9:30." Your list is two pages long. Send it?
You stay late on a floor emptied by the move. The motion-sensor lights shut off every three minutes. Keep waving your arms or go home?
A new teammate invites you to a quiz night "for bonding." The quiz is about the company's org structure. Go?
In the evening you review your task list: six tasks belong to a department that no longer exists. Close them or hand them off?
Your neighbor works for the same corporation in another building. In the evening he learns from you about a reorg that affects him too. Share details?
Late at night the team sends you a card: "Thanks for keeping us steady through the chaos." You're stuck in traffic, tearing up. Reply?
An anonymous employee channel posts a "leaked" new org chart in the evening. It looks real. Forward it to your team?
A new poster by the elevators: "Our Values: Courage. Openness. Alignment." Under "Courage," in small print: "within approved authority." Post a photo in chat?
The Culture team asks everyone to pick a "value of the day" and wear the matching pin. You choose "Self-care." There's no such pin. What do you wear?
8:45 a.m., over the loudspeakers: company calisthenics set to the corporate anthem. The whole floor stands up. You have a client call in one minute. Join in?
Culture launches a contest for a new verse of the company anthem. Prize: a day off. The only rhyme you have is "synergy" and "energy." Enter?
The intranet got a redesign: to find a colleague's phone number you now go through "Our Success Stories." Six clicks and a video. Still calling?
At a new-hire session you're asked to recite the company mission. All you remember is the word "Future," capitalized. Go for it?
right: Admit it and read from your phone

text: The intranet now has a "Kudos Wall," and the most-thanked people get bigger bonuses. Colleagues start trading kudos by arrangement. Join in?
Your department's Values Ambassador scolds you: in a meeting you said "that's not my job," which violates the "We Are One Team" value. It really isn't your job. Your reply?
right: "Values aren't a reason to do others' work"

text: Your idea to cut down on mass emails has 2,000 likes on the "Idea Bank." Status: "Under review" — for eighteen months. Nudge?
right: Resubmit it as a new idea

text: You're invited to star in a company values video. You'd smile at the camera and say, "I'm proud to work here." They promise just a few takes. Agree?
On the internal job board you stumble on an ad for your own position. Not a word about you. Ask your boss?
The evening newsletter "Value of the Month: Work-Life Balance" arrived at 11:47 p.m. Sender: the HR director. Reply?
At home you notice you've stuck a to-do list on the fridge in "Goal — Action — Value" format. Your partner asks if you're okay. Your answer?
The intranet crashes the instant you submit your vacation request. It's "processing" and can't be cancelled. Wait or resubmit?
right: Wait and check in the morning

text: Your teenager quotes the company values on your lanyard: "Courage. Openness." He wants the courage to go to a concert on a school night. Let him?
left: Let him go, values are values

text: The portal demands a new password this morning: "at least 16 characters, no words, no consecutive digits, unlike your last 24." Make one up?
Brand forbids the old logo even on internal slides. Your morning deck is covered in it. You present in 30 minutes. Redo it?
An enthusiastic colleague brings mugs printed with company values and hands them out. Yours says "Nothing Is Impossible." Drink from it?
right: Use it as a pencil cup

text: On the internal social network, your post about fixing the coffee machine gets more reactions than the VP's strategy post. His assistant asks you to delete it. Do you?
The portal has a "Suggest a portal improvement" form. It doesn't work. The only way to report that is through the form. What do you do?
The Chief Culture Officer runs a focus group: "What stops you from living our values?" You know the answer: focus groups. Say it?
Internal Comms is filming "A Day in the Life of an Employee." They picked you. You'd have to look upbeat from 9 to 6. Agree?
You search the knowledge base for how to file travel expenses. You find 14 instructions that contradict each other. Which do you follow?
The value of the quarter is "Speed." Meanwhile, the request for fast laptops for developers takes three months to approve. Point out the irony?
In the evening the portal sends your "Personal Recommendations": three courses, two posters and an article on "How Not to Burn Out." Sent at 10:15 p.m. Read it?
A designer friend looks at your company posters in the evening: "I could do better in one night." Recommend him to the Brand team?
In the evening Brand asks everyone to add the "corporate values frame" to their chat avatar. Yours is your cat. Change it?
left: Put the frame on the cat

text: You dream a values poster is demanding last quarter's report. You wake up at 2 a.m. What do you do?
left: Write down the dream and laugh

text: The elevator screen cycles through the company values. Slide six has a typo: "Accountabilty." Report it to Brand?
A vote for a "new company value" opens this morning. Options: "Innovation," "Innovativeness," "Innovative Thinking." Your pick?
Security asks you to remove the "Work Isn't Going Anywhere" poster from your desk because it "clashes with corporate style." It was a gift from your team. Take it down?
left: Take it down, keep it in a drawer

text: The company magazine wants to interview you on the value of "Openness." The press office sends you pre-written answers. Read them out?
You're writing through the portal, and it logs you out every two minutes "for security." The draft vanishes. Third attempt. What now?
You're given the "Values Champion of the Year" award. The ceremony is in the canteen; the trophy is plastic. You didn't prepare a speech. What do you say?
A colleague publicly calls your report "very strong," then DMs that it's all wrong. Behind him, a poster: "Honesty." What do you do?
In the evening you remember you promised the kids a poster for a school contest. All you have are spare company values posters. Use the backs?
For some reason, you come up with a better slogan than the official one: "We Do, Not Discuss." Submit it to the Idea Bank?
In the morning a robot vacuum with a "I Value Cleanliness" sticker gets stuck by your desk, beeping. Facilities opens at ten. What do you do?
Morning survey: "Do you know the company values by heart?" The only option for an honest "no" is "Still learning." Your answer?
right: Cram them in 10 minutes, say yes

text: You get a new badge with "your personal value" printed under your photo, chosen by an algorithm: "Patience." Wear it?
The morning company paper features a photo of your team captioned "Most Engaged." You're yawning in it. Ask for a different photo?
right: Pin the clipping to your desk

text: Culture introduces a morning ritual: everyone posts "My main goal today" in chat. You honestly want to write "survive till lunch." Do you?
The receptionist is rehearsing the official greeting, "Welcome to the Future!" and asks you to listen and rate it. You're running late. Listen?
The elevator plays an instrumental company anthem from 8 a.m. By the 40th floor you realize you're humming it. So is the colleague next to you. Sing louder?
In the company gym, a poster reads "Strength Is Our Value." You only have enough strength to sit on a machine and scroll your phone. Stay?
On the company shuttle home, two people from another team trash the "values" mercilessly. One of them wrote the poster. Join in?
An evening workshop, "Values Through Painting," promises to "reduce stress." Three hours. You just wanted to lie down. Go?
right: Lie down, that reduces stress too

text: At dinner you tell friends about the values posters. A friend from a small firm says: "We have one value — paying on time." Feel envious?
9:30 p.m. The portal sends an auto-task: "Share a story of how you lived the value of Care." Due today. Write it?
At dinner, the waiter says, "We value your openness." You instinctively look around for a poster. Time for a break?
8:55 a.m. The turnstile flashes red: your badge is "blocked due to quarterly activation expiry." About thirty people are queued behind you. What now?
right: Ask a colleague to swipe you in

text: The badge office opens at 9:00 and issues temporary passes only with a passport. Yours is at home. Go back for it?
right: Work from the café across the street

text: The guard at the entrance has known your face for five years but won't let you in without a badge: "Rules are the same for everyone." Try to charm him?
The lobby has 24 elevators, but only two serve your floor, and both are under inspection. Meeting in seven minutes. Climb to 22?
Your spot in the company garage is taken by a car with a "VP Temporary Pass" sticker. Parking elsewhere means a fine. What do you do?
The face recognition system mistakes you for a colleague from the 9th floor and grants you his access zones. Archive access would come in handy. Report it?
8:20 a.m. Breakfast is served until 8:30, but canteen badges activate at 8:30. The canteen guard shrugs. Do you eat?
A courier can't bring you a package: he needs a one-day pass, which must be ordered 24 hours ahead. It's samples for your 11 a.m. meeting. What do you do?
The morning train is packed with your own colleagues; half the car gets off at the company stop. Today you're squished against your boss. Start a conversation?
The coat check holds 400 coats for 6,000 people. It's full by 9:00. You're holding your puffer jacket. Where does it go?
right: Leave it with a friend at reception

text: Security is doing routine bag checks this morning. Your container of buckwheat looks suspicious and is sent for inspection. What do you say?
right: Crack a joke about the buckwheat

text: The entry system logs you at 9:01 and flags you as late. You were in line since 8:50. Dispute it?
Your badge won't open the meeting room you booked for 9:30. The guests are already in the hallway. How do you handle it?
left: Hold the meeting on the couches
right: Hunt down security with a key

text: 12:30. The canteen line stretches from the counter to the elevators. You have a 30-minute lunch and a call at 1 p.m. Wait it out?
The canteen cook recognizes you and saves you the last portion of cottage cheese pancakes. The colleague behind you wanted them too. Give them up?
right: Eat them, they were for you

text: The canteen installed a "smart register" that recognizes dishes from photos. It thinks your salad is a 900-ruble cake. Argue with the machine?
right: Pay and keep the line moving

text: You've found the only free table by the window. A department head sits down with her tray. Talk shop while you eat?
For the third week running the canteen menu features the "Corporate Cutlet." Culture asks for feedback on the food. Be honest?
The lobby coffee shop has a 20-minute line. A teammate suggests you get coffee for everyone if you stand in line for both of you. Do it?
You get stuck in an elevator between floors 17 and 18 with a lawyer who's ignored your email for a week. The dispatcher says 20 minutes. Bring up the email?
You're summoned to Finance's secure floor. Phones must go into a locker. You have an important call in 15 minutes. Go?
left: Hand over the phone and go
right: Ask them to come down to you

text: There's a line of eight at the floor's microwave. Each person heats for three minutes. Your lunch is going cold. Wait?
left: Wait and chat with the line

text: The floor guard asks you to remove the sticky notes from your monitor: "Clean desk policy." They have your passwords on them. Take them down?
The lounge has a new massage chair. Booking is through the portal; the only free slot is 2:15 p.m., during your stand-up. Book it?
left: Skip the stand-up for the chair
right: Give the slot to a colleague

text: The neighboring team eats lunch at their desks, and the smell of fish fills the open space. Culture is silent. Talk to them?
You head out for lunch and security asks to see your laptop bag. Inside: lunch and a laptop with no exit pass. What now?
The ground-floor mailroom has a package with your name on it, but they'll only release it to "the recipient with a power of attorney from themselves." Do it?
The vending machine ate your cash and gave you no chocolate. You can file a refund through the portal; review takes 30 days. File it?
7:10 p.m. The exit turnstile won't respond. Security says, "The system thinks you never came in." This morning you tailgated through someone else's gate. Confess?
In the evening, the canteen sells lunch leftovers at a discount. Half the office is lined up with containers. You promised to cook dinner at home. Buy some?
The night guard walks the floor switching off lights: "Energy-saving policy, after 9 p.m." You're mid-spreadsheet. What do you do?
In the evening the garage barrier won't lift: "Monthly exit limit exceeded." The limit is 20, and it's the 21st. How do you get out?
8:30 p.m. Fire drill. Walk down from the 33rd floor and check in outside. You were about to leave anyway. Combine?
In the evening the cleaner asks you to clear your desk for "scheduled deep cleaning." Your papers for tomorrow's board meeting are spread out. What do you do?
right: Ask her to clean around them

text: The last company shuttle leaves at 7:30. It's 7:25, and it's a five-minute run. Sending the email takes two more. What matters more?
left: Finish the email, take a taxi

text: In the evening you realize your key is locked inside, and your badge doesn't open the door after 7 p.m. Your coat is in there. Call someone?
Your neighbor raves about your office having its own canteen, gym and shuttle. You remember the line, the turnstile and the cutlet. Tell the truth?
The security patrol finds an unlocked drawer at your desk. You get a message: "Security violation, acknowledge and sign." Sign it?
The gym is open till 10 p.m., but after 8 entry is by booking only, and bookings close at 7. It's 7:05. What now?
The quarterly town hall this morning: 40,000 online, 2,000 in the hall. The CEO asks, "Any questions?" Silence. You have one. Raise your hand?
The town hall moderator wants "comfortable questions" for the CEO in advance. Yours is uncomfortable — about bonuses. Send it anyway?
right: Send a safe one on strategy

text: At the town hall, your neighbor dozes off and starts tipping onto your shoulder. The camera operator swings your way. Wake him?
right: Lend a shoulder, hold your breath

text: Colleagues hand out "town hall bingo" cards: "synergy," "challenges," "we're a family." First full row wins a pastry. Play?
The morning town hall streams on every screen, including the elevator and above the urinals. The sound can't be turned off. What do you do?
Comms wants you to share "your team's success story" live at the town hall in 90 seconds. You go on in 40 minutes. Do it?
In the morning Legal returns yesterday's email "Thanks, see you at 11" with edits: "We suggest: 'Thank you; meeting tentatively at 11:00, non-binding.'" Send it?
New rule: every external email goes through Legal. The client has been waiting since 8 a.m. for "Yes, received." The lawyer is stuck in traffic. What do you do?
A "legal bot" now scans email. It blocked your "Good morning!" as an "unverified claim about the quality of the morning." What do you write?
right: File a complaint about the bot

text: Legal wants a 600-word disclaimer on all your emails. Your average email is 30 words. Comply?
A junior lawyer reviewing your email sends back 17 clarifying questions. The email moves a meeting by 15 minutes. Answer?
You tell a client you've "attached the file." Legal changes it to "attached a file whose contents do not constitute an offer." The client calls, offended. What do you say?
Everyone's moving from email to chat to dodge Legal review. Now the lawyers have joined all the chats. What do you do?
The CEO called your town hall question "very brave." By lunch your boss has asked three times if "everything's okay." Your reply?
A lawyer now sits in every meeting and says "We need that on record" after each sentence. Meetings run three times longer. How do you run yours?
You're assigned the town hall minutes. The CEO spoke for two hours, half of it jokes Legal asks to "leave off the record." What stays in?
Legal approved a new email signature: name, title, four phone numbers, three warnings and a QR code to the privacy policy. It's longer than your emails. Use it?
After the town hall, the CEO has lunch in the staff canteen and sits at your table. Your colleagues freeze. Who speaks first?
A compliance officer asks you to replace "we guarantee" with "we will use reasonable efforts." The email is a birthday card for a colleague. Change it?
In the evening you watch the town hall replay at 2x. The CEO sounds like a cartoon. You're laughing as your partner walks in. Explain?
At 10 p.m. Legal replies: "Your email is approved, but it's been six hours since approval, so we'll recheck in the morning." The client needed it today. What now?
left: Send it after the morning check

text: Evening survey: "How inspired were you by the town hall?" The scale goes from "Very" to "Incredibly." You pick…
A childhood friend texts, "How are you?" You start replying and catch yourself waiting for Legal to approve. Legal isn't in this chat. How do you write?
In the evening, they announce anonymous questions for the next town hall. Your IT colleague whispers that the anonymity is "relative." Send a question?
In the evening you accidentally forward Legal an email where you call them "the Department of Delay." No undo. What now?
At 9 p.m. Comms asks you to proofread tomorrow's town hall slides. There are 180. The show's in the morning. Do it?
You email a colleague "You're a genius!" after he saves your skin. A minute later, an auto-warning: "Value judgments require legal review." How do you thank him?
left: Call and say it out loud

text: In the family chat you type "Buy milk." A second later, your hand reaches to add "non-binding, within a reasonable time." Vacation time?
At a bar, a lawyer friend from Legal admits he doesn't read 90% of emails and marks them "reviewed" by keyword. Find out the keywords?
The host warns you just five minutes ahead: you'll be on the big screen as "Employee of the Quarter." You're in an old sweater. What do you do?
Legal wants your email re-approved because you cc'd someone who "legally cannot be cc'd." They won't say who. How do you figure it out?
right: Send it to just one person

text: After the town hall comes the digest "The CEO's Top 10 Ideas." Idea #6 is the one you posted in the Idea Bank last week. No credit. Speak up?
A lawyer from upstairs comes in person to ask you not to write "urgent" in subject lines: "It creates legal expectations." You write it in every email. Your reply?
During the break a VP asks you what people "really" think about the strategy. Tell the truth?
The 360 review kicks off: 12 colleagues rate you, and you rate 23 people. Forty questions each. Start this morning?
The HR business partner sends the "talent matrix." You're in the "Reliable Performer" box. The next box over is "Future Leader." Ask for a review?
The portal updated pay grades. Your intern landed one grade above you due to a "market adjustment." He's in shock himself. What do you do?
Goal-setting season. You need five "ambitious but achievable" goals. Last year you set five and hit two. How do you set them now?
After calibration, your manager says: "Your rating was lowered because the department has to fit the curve." You did well. Push back?
The company paid for a coach. First session: 8 a.m. The coach asks, "What do you really want from life?" You wanted coffee. Answer honestly?
The 360 form on your boss asks, "What should he change?" Anonymity is guaranteed, but there are only three of you in the team. Be honest?
HR publishes new career tracks: the next level requires "cross-functional project experience" and a "values certificate." You have neither. Start collecting?
HR's morning pulse: "How likely are you to recommend the company to friends?" Yesterday you talked a friend out of applying. Score?
At 8:30 your boss asks for a self-assessment by lunch: "Don't be modest, but don't overdo it." How do you write it?
At your review the boss reads peer feedback: "Sometimes too blunt." It's from someone you bluntly saved from disaster. What do you say?
You've been added to the talent pool. That means evening courses, extra project work and a two-day assessment center. Stay in?
One of your people asks for a top rating: "I need a mortgage, the bank looks at bonuses." His work was average. Your call?
At manager training you learn the "feedback sandwich": praise, critique, praise. Your team already spots the sandwich from the first word. Use it?
HR says your rating has been "under review" for two months, and your bonus is on hold because of it. Time to escalate?
A colleague asks for a glowing review in the rating system: "And I'll do the same for you. Deal?" You're not sure he deserves it. Agree?
HR wants your individual development plan by Friday. The template has a field: "Hobbies useful to the company." Your hobby is growing tomatoes. Put it down?
After reviews, there's a confidential ranking of employees. A colleague shows you she can access it. Peek at your spot?
Your internal promotion interview is at 3 p.m. in a glass-walled room. Your current boss sits right across and sees everything. Go?
HR invites you to take two mentees in the mentoring program. It's four extra hours a week, but "it'll count in your review." Take them?
The annual certification includes an oral exam on policies. One of the three examiners wrote them and loves trick questions. Prepare?
HR launches a "benefits menu": gym, family health insurance or English classes. You must choose by 4 p.m. today. What do you pick?
In the evening you finish your self-assessment and realize you did way more this year than you remembered. Send it to your boss with a note?
Late at night you're writing a 360 review for someone you've met twice. The system won't accept blank fields. What do you write?
At 11 p.m. HR sends your review results: "Meets Expectations." Open the details now or in the morning?
Your friend, a psychologist, asks in the evening why a letter grade has you so stressed. You can't explain that a "B+" is basically a tragedy. Open up?
In the evening managers' chat, someone suggests giving the low ratings to people on parental leave. You're against it. Say so?
The evening "Leadership for High Potentials" course is taught by someone who changed jobs three times this year. Topic: "Staying with one system for the long haul." Pay attention?
Your kid gets a B at school and is upset. You remember your own "Meets Expectations." How do you comfort them?
Your boss texts in the evening: "Hey, I rated you a bit lower than I wanted. I'll explain later." When is "later"?
In the evening, your old classmates brag about promotions in a group chat. You've been "Senior Specialist" for three years. Post something?
At the end of review season you notice you're sleeping five hours a night. Tomorrow's the final calibration that decides your rating. Sleep early or prep?
One of your people texts in the evening: she got a low rating and is crying. It came from her matrix manager, not you. Call her?
right: Text, set a meeting for morning

text: After your final review meeting you step outside into the first snow. Walk the 40 minutes home or take a taxi?
At 9 p.m. the HR portal reminds you: "You haven't rated 4 colleagues. This will be reflected in your rating." It's an hour's work. Do it now?
The tender committee demands a tender for printer paper. Minimum three bidders. There's only one paper supplier in town. What do you do?
left: Find two more in other cities

text: A vendor sends a fruit basket "to celebrate our partnership." The gift policy allows up to 3,000 rubles. This looks pricier. What do you do?
right: Put it in the kitchen for everyone

text: Your flight is at 6:40 a.m. Policy allows economy only, and connecting flights if the direct one costs 10% more. It costs 11% more. Take the connection?
On the plane, your seatmate is from another department, flying to the same meeting for his own tender. Three hours side by side. Talk shop?
In the morning at the hotel you find the booking is in your name — for last month. No rooms. The corporate travel agent replies "within 48 hours." What now?
right: Wait in the lobby with your laptop

text: Procurement sends the spec for your new team's furniture: 40 chairs, all one color. Your team voted for multicolored. Fight for it?
The airport taxi must be booked via the corporate app, which offers a car in 40 minutes. Your flight is in 90. Book a regular one?
left: Book a regular one, argue later

text: A colleague on the tender whispers: one bidder is the deputy director's relative, and his bid somehow arrived before the tender was announced. What do you do?
Hotel breakfast isn't covered by your per diem. The buffet costs your entire daily allowance. A colleague suggests "eating for two days." Your move?
The tender portal crashes an hour before the deadline. Your supplier couldn't upload documents. Extensions go through the committee. What do you do?
Accounting rejects your expense report: the café receipt says "business lunch," not "lunch." They call it "entertainment." Argue?
At a meeting a vendor offers "a personal bonus" if you pick his company. You smile, but your stomach clenches. Your reply?
right: Joke it off, change the subject

text: A colleague on the trip asks you to put his dinner on your expense report: "My limit's used up, yours isn't." Small amount. Agree?
The bid committee asks each member to declare no conflict of interest. One bidder is your former classmate. Disclose it?
The new laptop purchase for your team is in month four. The approved model has been discontinued. Start over?
The office coffee supplier changed to the tender winner. The new coffee tastes like cardboard. The team is groaning. Complain to Procurement?
On the trip a local partner invites you to an expensive restaurant "as is tradition." The hospitality limit is 1,500 rubles. Go?
left: Go and pay your own way

text: You find the same monitor in a regular store for half the tender supplier's price. Policy forbids buying retail. Report it?
You've lost an 800-ruble taxi receipt. Without it, you need a written explanation to the CFO. Write it?
The cleaning contract went to a company that mops once a week. Employees start bringing their own mops. Join them?
Evening on a business trip. Colleagues invite you to a local museum; your report for HQ isn't done. The museum closes at eight. Where to?
Your return flight is delayed to 11:40 p.m. Meeting at 9 tomorrow. You could switch to a morning flight but miss the meeting. Which?
right: Fly in the morning, be late

text: No Wi-Fi in your hotel room tonight, and the report must go through the corporate VPN. The lobby is open till midnight. Go down?
left: Sit in the lobby till midnight

text: Before leaving the trip you want to get souvenirs for the team. Policy says no expensing them. Buy with your own money?
You get home from the trip at 10 p.m. Family's waiting, but there are 140 emails, three marked "yesterday." Open them?
In the evening the expense system says you're 37 rubles over the limit and blocks the entire 42,000-ruble report. What do you do?
At 9 p.m. the corporate travel agency sends tomorrow's tickets — in your colleague's name. Departure 7 a.m. Call the agency?
right: Buy your own, claim it later

text: Your partner asks why you brought 12 hotel shampoos back from the trip. You honestly don't know. Confess?
Lodging policy put you in a room with a colleague from another department. He snores, and you present in the morning. What do you do?
At 8 p.m. a bidder sends a 60-page clarification. Policy says reply within 24 hours. Start tonight?
The morning after you're back, you owe a trip report: "Goals, results, company impact." You went to sign a paper that could've been mailed. What do you write?
At 7 a.m. the hotel wants payment for a minibar you never touched. Accounting won't reimburse minibar charges. Argue before your taxi comes?
The new stationery supplier delivers pens that only write if you press with both hands. The contract runs three years. How do you cope?
8 a.m. Your calendar has 11 meetings today, three overlapping, and one titled just "Meeting," with no description or organizer. Which first?
The Vladivostok branch books a call at 7 a.m. your time — their end of day. Third time this week. Agree?
left: Get up at six and join

text: You booked a room for 9 a.m. two weeks ago. At 9, a VP is sitting in it with his own meeting, peering at you over his glasses. What do you do?
The daily stand-up is supposed to take 15 minutes. Yours hit 55 because two people argued about fonts. You're running it. Cut them off?
left: Cut them off and wrap up

text: You've been invited to a 46-person meeting "for information." You have no idea why. Decline without explanation?
One of your people asks to move your regular one-on-one: "Nothing to discuss, all's fine." That's the fifth time in a row. Insist?
Morning call with HQ. Your neighbor's renovation is in full swing — hammer drill on max. Camera required. What do you do?
Morning invite: "Meeting on Reducing Meeting Time." Length: three hours. You're a required attendee. Go?
The director's assistant moves your meetings without asking: "He needs a window." Your client meeting slid onto your lunch. Object?
The corporation spans 11 time zones. A meeting says "9:00," but whose nine? You arrive to an empty room. Wait?
right: Leave and wait for a new invite

text: At a meeting without an agenda, everyone spends 40 minutes debating what the agenda should be. Take the lead?
Partners from the London office want a "quick call." Their "quick" is 90 minutes with an English deck. You're at lunch. Agree?
After the meeting nobody wants to write the minutes. Everyone looks at you because "you phrase things best." Do it?
Two groups booked the 30-person room for the same slot. Both groups are yours. How do you sort it?
right: One gets the room, one the canteen

text: On a video meeting, everyone's camera is on except the CEO's. The moderator asks you to turn yours on. You're in a home hoodie. Turn it on?
At 2 p.m. a meeting pops up: "Urgent, 5 min," from the department head. You're the only invitee. What do you do?
right: Ask in chat what it's about

text: A weekly meeting has run for two years, though the project it was for has closed. Everyone keeps showing up. Propose cancelling?
On an international video call, the interpreter translates your joke so that colleagues in Asia stare in horror. Explain?
The only free meeting room is windowless, unventilated and seats four. There are seven of you. Two-hour meeting. Go?
left: Go in, prop the door open

text: The meeting set for 5:30 is still going at 7:15. No one dares say it's time to go home. Will you?
The US office invites you to an 11 p.m. meeting — "it's only an hour." You have an early train. Accept?
In the evening you look at tomorrow: nine meetings, no time for actual work. Block two hours of "Focus" time?
right: Leave it open, just in case

text: Evening call, you're on camera, and your kid charges into frame in a dinosaur costume. The meeting freezes. What do you do?
At 9 p.m. you realize you never sent the morning's meeting minutes, which include three tasks due tomorrow. Send them now?
In the evening a colleague moves tomorrow's meeting to 7:30 "to get it done before work." He's a morning person. You're not. Agree?
After the meeting, attendees keep debating in chat. 200 messages this evening. Read them all?
For the first time this week, an evening with no meetings. The phone is quiet. You feel uneasy, like you've missed something. How do you spend it?
A meeting with the Asia office is set for 4 a.m. The CEO wants "a live person from our side." Volunteer?
Your partner asks you not to bring the laptop to bed, but you present at 8 a.m. and the slides aren't done. What do you do?
right: Sleep now, get up at six

text: The corporate wellbeing program sets everyone a 10,000-step daily goal. The company wristband reports to HR. It's 8 a.m. and you're at 12 steps. Walk?
right: Shake the band on the subway

text: Employee Care launches "morning meditation" at 8:30 in the big room. Your meeting there starts 15 minutes later, and you still need to set up chairs. Meditate?
The kindergarten is unexpectedly closed for disinfection. The office has a "parents' room," but it has to be booked a week ahead. What do you do?
left: Bring the kid to the office

text: In the morning your cat lay on the laptop and sent 400 letter z's to the all-staff chat. 1,200 people. Explain?
Alarm at 6 a.m. You went to bed at 1 after clearing your inbox. You could sleep 40 more minutes and skip corporate yoga, which earns "Care Points." Sleep?
A neighbor who works for the same corporation offers you a lift every morning. On the way he talks about his KPIs. Accept?
The employee support hotline offers a first session at 9 a.m. You've been meaning to. But you sign up through your direct manager. Do it?
At breakfast you're feeding the family and answering emails. Your son asks you to listen to his poem for class. Put the phone down?
The upstairs neighbors flooded you this morning. The plumber will come "between 9 and 6." You have a key meeting with a VP today. What do you do?
right: Go in, ask neighbors to wait

text: The new "recovery room" has a sleep pod. Twenty-minute slots. It's free now, but you have a call in 20 minutes. Nap?
right: Give the slot to a colleague

text: At 1 p.m. the teacher calls: your kid got into a fight, you need to come in. You present at 2 — a month of prep. What do you do?
Your boss read an article on burnout and now asks the team every hour: "How do you feel on a scale of 1 to 10?" The team is fed up. Tell him?
Corporate fitness challenge: departments compete in planking. Yours is losing because of you — you last 20 seconds. Train at lunch?
You realize you've had lunch standing by the printer three days running. A colleague suggests lunch in the park. Call in 40 minutes. Go?
Mom calls during a meeting for the fourth time. She never calls during the day. Step out and answer?
Health & Safety checks your ergonomics: wrong chair, monitor too low, and you "sit like a comma." A new chair takes three months through Procurement. What do you do?
You have a splitting headache, and the floor's first-aid kit is locked. The office manager with the key is in meetings until 4 p.m. What now?
Massage therapists are in the office for a day. Booking filled in 4 minutes. Your colleague got a slot but was called to the director's. He offers it to you. Take it?
right: Give it to the next in line

text: Evening corporate yoga at 7 p.m. The instructor says, "Let go of work thoughts." Your phone buzzes. Look?
Today is your daughter's birthday; the party starts at 7. At 6:40 the boss asks for a "quick look" at a contract. Quick means an hour. What do you do?
Your partner made dinner and lit candles. Five minutes in: "Urgent: report rejected." Open it?
At night you lie awake replaying tomorrow's meeting with Legal, Finance and Compliance. Sleep won't come. What do you do?
left: Write it down and let go

text: The company gives you a pool pass — for a pool across town that closes at 8 p.m. You leave the office at 7:30. Try to make it?
right: Give the pass to a neighbor

text: Your kid asks if you can go to the zoo on Saturday. Saturday you have a "voluntary" project day. Promise?
You're finally on vacation, on the beach. A colleague writes: "Sorry to bother you on holiday, but where's the contract file?" You know instantly. Reply?
The company band pings: "You average 5 hours 12 minutes of sleep. Data shared with the wellbeing program." Take it off?
right: Go to bed early for the stats

text: Friends invite you to their country house Friday evening. You've already cancelled twice for work. Friday is the annual budget deadline. Go?
In the evening you notice the guitar you haven't played in a year. You could play for half an hour or clear your inbox. Which?
An off-site team building is announced: ropes course, rafting and a "trust campfire." Bus leaves Saturday at 6 a.m. Attendance "encouraged." Go?
You've been put in charge of the department's New Year party for 300. The budget's been cut by two-thirds. First planning meeting at 9. Your pitch?
The company announces a volunteer day: plant trees or help sort records at an animal shelter. You must go, but you can choose. Which?
A colleague is collecting 2,000 rubles a head for the boss's milestone birthday. Payday is a week away. Chip in?
Compliance asks you to declare this year's gifts. You recall: a supplier's calendar, a client's chocolate bar and a key ring from a competitor. Declare all?
You learn that a colleague from another team expenses rides home as "client meetings." There's an anonymous hotline. Call it?
At the morning corporate run the photographer asks everyone to smile in front of the logo banner. You're at kilometer five and look like a lemon. Pose?
Culture announces "Best Office": decorate your workspace in brand colors. Colleagues are already buying garlands. Join in?
At the team-building, teams are assigned at random. Yours is the people you haven't spoken to since an old project. What do you do?
The emcee calls you on stage for the "Guess the Department by Its Sound" contest. The whole hall applauds. Go?
right: Decline, say you've lost your voice

text: At the team-building, colleagues prank you: you've "won a company trip." You almost believed it. Get upset?
right: Ask them not to do that

text: A client sends you a fancy pen in a box. Policy says gifts over 3,000 rubles go back. It's your dream pen. What do you do?
A colleague complains to you about the boss and asks you to back his HR complaint. It's mostly fair, but the boss values you. Sign?
right: Suggest he talk to the boss

text: Company Day relay race. Your team is on the final leg, and it's yours. You're in office shoes. Run?
right: Hand off to someone in sneakers

text: The team is preparing a song about the department for the party. You got the verse about policies. It's a solo. Agree?
Your sister started a catering firm and asks how to get into the tender for your company's party. You're on the organizing committee. Help her?
At the team-building your raft flips. Everyone's soaked; the boss laughs loudest. Suggest switching rafts?
In Secret Santa you drew a VP. Budget: 1,000 rubles. What do you give?
After volunteer day you need a report with photos and "social impact." You hauled bags all day. Write a long one?
The party is in full swing. You're tired; colleagues pull you onto the dance floor. The boss is already dancing. Stay or slip away?
In the evening 600 party photos hit the group chat. Your eyes are closed in 40 of them. Ask to delete some?
In the evening you get an anonymous message: "Your manager falsifies reports. I have proof." What do you do?
After the party, the company bus drops people off until 2 a.m. You're the last stop. Ride or pay for a taxi?
After the party, there's a mountain of leftover food. Policy says dispose of it. Colleagues propose taking it to a shelter. Help load it?
left: Help take it to the shelter

text: The evening before the boss's birthday, it turns out nobody bought the gift. Shops close in 30 minutes. You're nearby. Save the day?
In the evening at the off-site, colleagues play a board game for forfeits. The loser sings the company anthem solo. Play?
The evening after the party, Culture posts a video of you singing. It already has 3,000 views. Ask them to take it down?
right: Like it and embrace the fame

text: In the evening you remember you broke a paddle at the off-site, and no one noticed. The company paid for the rental. Report it?
Starting Monday the whole company moves to a new ERP. The old one went dark at 7 a.m.; the new one comes up "during the day." A client invoice is due by 10. What do you do?
left: Make it by hand in a spreadsheet

text: You filed an IT ticket: "Mouse not working." Three days later: "Ticket closed. Reason: user didn't answer a follow-up question." There was no question. What now?
In the morning the VPN wants an SMS code, which goes to your work phone. It's at the office. You're home. What do you do?
The company is piloting an AI assistant that writes emails "in corporate style." It turns your "Hi, send me the file" into 120 words. Send it?
In the morning your laptop decides to install a two-hour update. Can't cancel — "security policy." You present in 20 minutes. What do you do?
The system wants a new password that matches none of your last 24. Your imagination ran dry at number 18. What do you do?
After the data migration, every client's name is garbled with stray accented letters. Angry emails pour in. Who fixes it?
Two-factor authentication pinged your old number, which you changed a year ago. To update it, you have to log in. Call IT?
Monday morning: the mail server "migrated" and all weekend email vanished. Your boss texts: "Did you get my email on Saturday?"
You've been named a "super user" of the new system. Now everyone calls you instead of support. Thirty-four calls today. What do you do?
The new ERP training is online: 12 hours of video. The trainer is using an old version of the interface. Watch it?
The internal HR chatbot answers "How many vacation days do I have?" with "Our company values caring for you." Ask again?
You need access to a shared folder. The request form asks for the "resource owner." The owner left in 2019. Whom do you list?
An internal hackathon is announced: 48 hours for a "breakthrough idea." The winner gets implementation and a certificate. Your team is fired up. Join?
Your boss wants the AI assistant writing your reports. The result is upbeat — and invents three clients. Send it?
The printer only prints when you tap your badge. Since the reorg, it doesn't recognize yours. You need the document in 10 minutes. What do you do?
left: Ask a colleague to print it

text: Security ran a phishing drill. You clicked. Now you owe a "How Not to Click" course and a written explanation. Tell the team?
You're asked to test a new ERP module "in your spare time." You find 46 bugs. Report them all?
New policy: no files on your desktop, cloud only. The cloud gives you 2 GB; your decks weigh 30. What do you do?
The overnight data load into the new system crashes every night at 11:40. You're on call. Restart it by hand until morning?
right: Email the vendor, go to sleep

text: In the evening the VPN won't work through your home router. IT says "restart the router," and someone at home is watching football. Restart?
10 p.m. notification: "Your computer will restart in 5 minutes." You have two hours of unsaved work open. What do you do?
In the evening you write to ERP support. A bot replies: "Thanks for reaching out! Expected response time: 11 business days." Wait?
left: Wait and work the old way

text: Your teenager looks at your company's system and says, "I could build better in a weekend." Let him take a look?
At 1 a.m. a server goes down and the work chat starts ringing. You're not on call, but you know a five-minute fix. Answer?
Your phone pings every minute this evening: the new ERP sends reminders about "pending actions." There are 312. What do you do?
7:30 p.m. The 600-seat open space is nearly empty. In a far corner, someone is crying over a spreadsheet. Go over?
right: Leave them be and go home

text: In the evening you're handed a bag of company swag: hoodie, thermos, logo socks. The socks are two sizes too small. What do you do?
left: Give the socks to the intern

text: The evening company digest: 64 news items. Item 58, in small print: "Canteen hours change Monday." You nearly missed it. Warn the team?
After 8 p.m. the motion sensors only respond to large objects. You sit still and end up in the dark. What do you do?
In the evening you notice the office ficus you've watered for two years is on the disposal list after the move. Take it home?
In the evening you notice the meeting room clock runs 20 minutes fast, so every meeting there ends early. Colleagues know and say nothing. Report it to Facilities?
In the evening the doorman tells you he's been here longer than half the departments have existed and remembers every CEO. Listen to his stories?
On your way out you spot your lunch box from last Friday in the fridge. Open it or toss it unseen?
In the mailroom this evening there's a parcel for a long-gone colleague. Something inside is ticking. What do you do?
A cat has moved into the office, never officially registered. Facilities emails in the evening: "Cat not on the asset register, subject to eviction." The team is horrified. Step in?
left: Take the cat under your wing

text: Colleagues stay late for tea and gossip. You meant to leave, but the gossip is about your project. Stay?
A note appears on the board: "Whoever took my stapler, give it back, I know who you are." You have it. You took it by mistake. Return it?
For the first time in six months you wipe your desk and find a colleague's badge under the monitor — he's been looking for it for three months. Return it?
right: Drop it at the badge office

text: You're the last one out, and the guard asks you to sign the "Left after 9 p.m." log. Your name's already in it 18 times this month. Sign?
In the evening the floor's water cooler starts gurgling and leaking. Facilities closed at 6. The water is creeping toward a power strip. What do you do?
In the morning, 14 sticky notes from colleagues cover your monitor: "Call me," "Urgent," "Where's the report?" and one "You're great." Which first?
Every morning the next team does its stand-up at full volume right by your desk. Every day. What do you do?
In the morning you notice a typo on your name plate. Reprints go through Print Services — a month's wait. What do you do?
The floor's coffee machine shows "Service required." Twelve sleepy people are in line. You know where the reset button is. Press it?
left: Press it and be a hero

text: Hot-desking this morning gave you a desk by the kitchen. It smells of yesterday's fish. No other seats. How do you work?
Internal mail delivers an envelope sent from the next desk three weeks ago. Inside: an invite to a meeting that already happened. What do you do?
HR sends a memo: "Friday is casual day, within business style." You came in a reindeer sweater. Change?
You're on the phone in a glass meeting room when you realize a school tour of the office is staring at you. What do you do?
A colleague goes around collecting signatures on a card for someone you've never met, retiring after 40 years. What do you write?
The elevators are down, and you're climbing to the 29th floor with a box of paper. At the 15th, a courier passes you carrying two. Ask for help?
Someone opened a meeting room window for the first time — turns out they open. Fresh air, birds. Five minutes later Security arrives: "Climate control violation." Close it?
Next year's budget cycle starts. Finance wants a budget "with a buffer, but no buffer." The template has 19 tabs. Due Friday. Where do you start?
External auditors walk in this morning wanting "all contracts from the past three years, on paper." Half are in the e-archive. Print them?
The project steering committee meets at 8 a.m. You're presenting — last on an agenda of 15 items. Wait or ask to go first?
Outside consultants are interviewing about "department processes." Their draft contains your own slides from last year, with their logo on them. Point it out?
Risk asks you to update the project risk register every morning. It already lists 140 risks, the top one being "risk register not updated." Update it?
right: Add a risk about the register

text: At 8:15 the CFO asks you to cut your project budget by 20% "without losing results." You know it's impossible. Your answer?
Comms is preparing the annual report and wants your "biggest win of the year in one sentence." You can't choose. What do you write?
Last day of the quarter. Accounting wants all acts closed by noon. You have 18 open, six missing counterparty signatures. How do you save it?
The portfolio office wants to reclassify your project from "Strategic" to "Operational" this morning. That halves your resources. Fight it?
You find an error in the project's financial model: payback is eight years, not three. The project's already approved. Report it?
right: Quietly fix it in the next version

text: An auditor asks a question only your departed predecessor can answer. He now works for a competitor. Call him?
New cost-cutting: AC goes off at 4 p.m. It's July, and you have partner talks at 4:30. What do you do?
A neighboring department asks to "borrow" part of your budget until year-end, promising to repay next year. Those promises rarely hold. Lend it?
Internal Audit picked your department for a "random check." You need to assign someone to the auditors for two weeks. Who goes?
At the investment committee you're asked something answered on appendix slide 46. You don't remember it. How do you handle it?
The day before his report is due, a consultant asks you for "a bit of data." A bit means five years of exports. His report goes to the CEO. Help?
Finance allocated canteen costs by department. Yours got the biggest share, though your team eats at home. Dispute it?
In the plan-vs-actual review your numbers matched the plan to the ruble. Finance suspects fudging. You just planned well. How do you prove it?
You're unexpectedly called to the board meeting to answer one question. It comes after two hours in the waiting room. Wait?
right: Ask them to call when ready

text: At 9 p.m. Finance sends the "final" budget template. You'll have to re-enter all your numbers. Due at 9 a.m. Start now?
The auditors stay until 10 p.m. and want someone from your department with them. Everyone looks at you. Stay?
In the evening you review the year-end checklist: 300 items, 297 done. The last three depend on people on vacation. What do you do?
The consultant invites you to dinner "to talk informally." He wants his contract extended, and you're evaluating him. Go?
right: Go and pay your own way

text: A finance colleague calls at 8:40 p.m.: "Your budget's off by 14 rubles. I can't close without it." You're home. Search now?
right: Offer to look in the morning

text: At night it hits you how to cut department costs by 30% without firing anyone. Jot it down or sleep on it?
right: Get up and write it all out

text: An accountant friend calls: year-end close, she's basically living at the office. You understand each other perfectly. Invite her out this weekend?
right: Wish her strength, go to bed

text: Evening memo: "All business travel cancelled through year-end." Including tomorrow's trip to a key client. Request an exception?
In the evening an envelope marked "Confidential: 2027 budget cuts" turns up on your desk. It's addressed to your boss. What do you do?
In the morning they bring you a new hire: "He's onboarding with you for three months." This is the first you've heard. Your project is on fire. What do you do?
